newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Albright vows no concessions on NATO charter.
newsitem.headline: Albright vows no concessions on NATO charter.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright headed for Moscow on Thursday vowing no concessions over the terms of a NATO-Russia charter designed to compensate the Kremlin for NATO's eastward expansion.
"Basically, we are at our bottom line," Albright told reporters aboard the plane taking her to the Russian capital for a day of talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

The Western alliance and Russia hope to sign the charter on May 27, a few weeks before NATO announces at a Madrid summit which East European countries will be invited to join first. The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are front-runners.

The pact would give Moscow the right to close consultations with NATO on European security, but the alliance is refusing Russian demands for binding guarantees that no nuclear weapons or NATO troops will be stationed on new members' territory.
"We don't want to have any second class NATO membership, there can be no subordination of NATO to anybody," Albright said.
East European states, which have clamoured to join NATO since the collapse of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact, are sensitive about any limits on the terms of their membership.

NATO has said it has "no plan, no need and no intention" to place nuclear weapons in new member countries or permanently station substantial combat forces there. But Western leaders will not subscribe to a commitment never to do so.

Albright said she did not expect any "miraculous dawning" as a result of Thursday's talks. She and other U.S. officials were careful to stress that NATO's negotiations are led by Secretary- General Javier Solana, who will next meet Primakov in Luxembourg on May 6.
"What we hope to do is move it forward, keep it moving so Solana could pick it up from there," said U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
"If the Russians have questions that require further explanation, we will do further explaining, but we will not change the substance of our position."
NATO says it will go ahead with enlargement, with or without a deal with Russia.
In the lead-up to Albright's visit, Russian leaders have kept up a barrage of rhetoric against NATO expansion. U.S. officials expect it will continue even if a charter is signed.

After preliminary talks in Moscow on Wednesday with U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, Russia also signalled the importance of agreement on the related issue of force levels throughout Europe.
NATO and Russia are seeking to amend the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe treaty to reflect the end of the Cold War and remove the threat of a force build-up on Russia's borders.
Albright said Russia's stance was "normal negotiating tactics" and that she would again seek to convince Moscow "that an enlarged NATO is not an enlarged threat to Russia".
Albright described her visit as part of a series of meetings on the NATO issue she saw as necessary with Primakov with whom she said she had developed good working relations.

She said she considered it "polite" for her to travel to Moscow because of Primakov's recent gallstone surgery. Venues in Western Europe and the United States had earlier been discussed for the meeting.

It remained unclear whether Albright would meet Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who cut short a Black Sea holiday on Wednesday and returned to Moscow. She said she had all along planned to telephone him but awaited further word in Moscow.
